# Extending Transit Survey Yield Estimation with Correlated Noise and Radial Velocity Constraints

This paper presents an extension of the Pepper & Gaudi formalism for estimating transit survey yields in homogeneous stellar populations, with a particular focus on incorporating the effects of correlated noise on transit time-scales—an aspect not fully addressed in the original framework. This extension is essential for realistically modeling the performance of transit surveys, since correlated (or "red") noise sources, such as those arising from instrumental systematics or stellar variability, can significantly affect detection statistics in ways that differ from the assumptions of purely white (uncorrelated) noise.

In addition to accounting for correlated noise, the formalism developed here simultaneously incorporates magnitude limits imposed by the requirement for radial velocity (RV) follow-up of transit candidates. This is a critical consideration for real-world survey design, as the confirmation of planetary transit signals typically requires spectroscopic follow-up capable of detecting the corresponding RV signal, which is only feasible for sufficiently bright host stars. By jointly modeling these two effects—correlated noise and RV-driven magnitude limits—the framework provides a more complete and realistic picture of expected survey yields.

To achieve this, new analytical expressions are derived for the various noise contributions relevant on transit time-scales, along with a revised least-squares detection statistic tailored to the box-shaped transit profile characteristic of planetary transits. Furthermore, the dependence of these noise contributions and detection statistics on stellar mass is re-examined in detail, given that stellar mass strongly influences both the intrinsic photometric noise properties of a star and the amplitude of the RV signal induced by an orbiting planet.

A key finding of this analysis is that correlated noise components which remain constant with apparent stellar magnitude—rather than scaling down for brighter stars—induce a steep decline in detection probability at higher stellar masses. This effect arises because more massive stars produce shallower transit depths for a given planet size, making them more susceptible to the deleterious impact of correlated noise. When combined with the magnitude limits imposed by the need for RV confirmation, this decline in sensitivity can substantially curtail the practical effectiveness of transit surveys targeting star clusters, even when such clusters would otherwise appear to be promising targets based on their stellar density and photometric accessibility.

Despite these limitations, the analysis demonstrates that small-aperture, wide-field transit surveys retain the capability to successfully detect hot Neptune-type planets in very nearby star clusters, specifically those located within approximately 100 parsecs. In such cases, the resulting RV signals remain large enough to be measurable with current-generation spectroscopic instrumentation, thereby preserving the viability of these surveys for detecting close-in Neptune-sized planets despite the constraints imposed by correlated noise and follow-up requirements.

# Extending the Pepper & Gaudi Formalism for Transit Survey Yield Predictions in Homogeneous Stellar Populations

## Introduction

Ground-based transit surveys targeting star clusters and other homogeneous stellar populations offer a unique opportunity to study planet occurrence rates as a function of well-constrained stellar age, metallicity, and mass. However, accurately predicting the yield of such surveys requires careful modeling of the noise sources that limit detection sensitivity, as well as realistic accounting for the observational constraints imposed by follow-up requirements. The foundational framework developed by Pepper & Gaudi (2005) established analytic expressions for computing transit detection probabilities and expected planet yields for surveys targeting large ensembles of stars with a given luminosity function and spatial distribution. While this formalism has been widely adopted and adapted for various survey designs, it did not explicitly incorporate the effects of correlated (red) noise, nor did it jointly consider the constraints imposed by the need for radial velocity (RV) confirmation of transiting candidates.

In this study, we extend the Pepper & Gaudi formalism to address these two important considerations. First, we derive new analytic expressions for the contribution of correlated noise to the detection statistic, generalizing the standard signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) calculations that typically assume purely uncorrelated (white) noise. Second, we incorporate the requirement that candidate transiting planets be bright enough to permit RV mass measurements or confirmation, which imposes an effective magnitude limit on the sample of viable target stars. This magnitude limit depends on the RV facility employed, the mass and orbital period of the planet, and the properties of the host star, and can differ substantially from the magnitude limit set by photometric precision alone.

## Methodology

### Correlated Noise in the Detection Statistic

Standard treatments of transit detection statistics, including the original Pepper & Gaudi framework, typically assume that the dominant noise source is photon-limited (white) noise, whose variance decreases as the inverse of the number of photometric points combined in a transit. In practice, however, ground-based photometric time series are often affected by systematic, time-correlated noise arising from atmospheric effects, instrumental variations, and imperfect detrending algorithms. This correlated noise component does not average down with the number of data points in the same way as white noise, and its presence can substantially degrade the effective SNR of shallow transit signals, particularly for the small transit depths expected around larger, more massive stars.

We derive an updated expression for the least-squares detection statistic that explicitly separates the contributions of white and correlated noise components. This generalized formalism allows the total noise variance to be written as the sum of a term that scales with the number of in-transit photometric points (white noise) and a term that remains constant regardless of the number of points (correlated noise floor). We show how this decomposition propagates through the standard expressions for the minimum detectable transit depth and the resulting survey completeness fraction as a function of stellar mass, radius, and apparent magnitude.

### Radial Velocity Follow-up Constraints

In addition to detection via photometry, we incorporate the requirement that any transiting planet candidate be amenable to RV follow-up observations sufficient to confirm planetary nature and, ideally, measure the planet mass. This requirement imposes a magnitude limit that depends on the precision of available RV instrumentation, the exposure times required to reach that precision, and the expected RV semi-amplitude of the planet-star system. For a given planet mass and orbital period, we compute the maximum apparent magnitude for which a statistically significant RV detection is feasible, and we combine this limit with the photometric detection criteria described above to determine the joint probability of both transit detection and RV confirmation.

This joint treatment is particularly important for surveys targeting distant or compact stellar populations such as globular clusters, where the typical apparent magnitudes of cluster members may be too faint for RV follow-up even if the transit signal itself is photometrically detectable.

## Results

Applying this extended formalism to a range of representative survey configurations, we find that the inclusion of a magnitude-independent correlated noise floor has a pronounced effect on the predicted transit yield, especially for surveys targeting star clusters composed predominantly of higher-mass stars. Because the transit depth for a given planet radius decreases with increasing stellar radius, and because more massive main-sequence stars are systematically larger, the presence of a correlated noise floor disproportionately suppresses detectability around these stars. This effect becomes especially severe in clusters where a large fraction of the stellar population lies near or above one solar mass, sharply reducing the overall detection probability and, consequently, the expected planet yield.

This finding has direct implications for the design and interpretation of cluster-based transit surveys. Even in the idealized case of perfect photometric precision limited only by photon noise, the presence of a modest correlated noise floor —typical of ground-based instruments— can substantially curtail the population of stars for which transit signals of small planets are detectable. Surveys aiming to characterize planet occurrence in clusters must therefore account for this effect when estimating achievable sample sizes and statistical power.

Despite this limitation, our analysis identifies a promising niche for small-aperture, wide-field survey instruments: the detection of hot Neptune-sized planets around low-mass stars in nearby open clusters, specifically those within approximately 100 parsecs. For such nearby systems, the apparent brightness of cluster members is sufficient both to achieve adequate photometric SNR despite the correlated noise floor, and to permit RV mass measurements with existing or near-future spectroscopic facilities. This combination makes very nearby clusters attractive targets for surveys seeking to establish planet occurrence rates in coeval, well-characterized stellar populations, even though more distant or higher-mass-dominated clusters may be effectively inaccessible to the same survey strategy.

## Discussion and Conclusions

Our extension of the Pepper & Gaudi formalism provides a more realistic framework for forecasting the yield of ground-based transit surveys in star clusters and other homogeneous stellar populations, by jointly incorporating the effects of correlated photometric noise and the magnitude constraints imposed by RV follow-up. The results underscore the importance of considering both of these factors together, as neglecting either can lead to overly optimistic yield predictions.

The strong sensitivity of detection probability to stellar mass in the presence of correlated noise suggests that survey designers should carefully consider the mass function of their target population when planning cluster-based transit searches, favoring clusters dominated by lower-mass stars where possible. At the same time, our identification of nearby clusters as viable targets for hot Neptune detection with small-aperture instruments offers a concrete pathway for future observational programs, potentially enabling comparative studies of planet occurrence as a function of stellar age and environment using existing wide-field photometric facilities combined with moderate-aperture RV spectrographs.

Future work could extend this analysis to explore alternative detrending strategies aimed at mitigating the correlated noise floor, as well as to incorporate more detailed treatments of specific RV instrument capabilities and cluster membership uncertainties, further refining yield predictions for upcoming cluster transit surveys.

# Where Innovation Meets Timeless Art: Pepper Robot at Gaudi's Masterpieces

In an unexpected fusion of cutting-edge technology and century-old artistry, Barcelona has introduced something truly new to its cultural landscape: Pepper, the humanoid robot, now serves as an interactive guide at several of Antoni Gaudí's architectural masterpieces.

Standing at the entrance of Park Güell, Pepper greets visitors with its characteristic tablet display and gentle voice, offering multilingual explanations about the mosaic techniques, structural innovations, and philosophical inspirations that guided Gaudí's unconventional designs. The robot's presence represents a fascinating dialogue between two eras of innovation—Gaudí's revolutionary approach to architecture in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and today's advancement in artificial intelligence and robotics.

This pairing is more fitting than it might initially seem. Gaudí himself was a visionary who pushed boundaries, incorporating organic forms found in nature into his buildings long before such biomimicry became a recognized design philosophy. His work at Casa Batlló, Casa Milà, and the still-unfinished Sagrada Família broke conventions and embraced experimentation—qualities that resonate with Pepper's own role as a pioneer in human-robot interaction.

Visitors have responded positively to this new addition to the cultural experience. Children especially seem captivated by conversing with Pepper while learning about the intricate ceramic work and gravity-defying columns that define Gaudí's style. The robot can point out details easily missed by the human eye, share historical anecdotes, and even respond to questions in real-time, creating a more personalized and engaging tour experience.

Some purists have raised concerns about technology overshadowing the organic, handcrafted nature of Gaudí's work. They argue that introducing robotic elements into spaces designed to evoke natural forms and spiritual contemplation creates an odd juxtaposition. Others counter that this pairing actually enhances accessibility, making the complex historical and architectural context available to a broader, more diverse audience, including younger generations who connect naturally with interactive technology.

The pepper plant itself—the spice from which the robot borrows its name—offers an interesting metaphor here. Just as peppers add complexity and unexpected zest to cuisine, this technological addition introduces new layers of engagement to the appreciation of classical architecture. It's a reminder that innovation, whether in cooking, robotics, or architectural design, often comes from combining seemingly disparate elements to create something entirely new.

As cities worldwide grapple with how to make historical and cultural sites more accessible and engaging for contemporary audiences, Barcelona's experiment with Pepper at Gaudí's sites may offer valuable insights. It demonstrates that reverence for the past and embrace of the future need not be mutually exclusive—sometimes the most meaningful cultural experiences emerge precisely at that intersection.

# Abstract

We present an extension of the analytic transit survey yield formalism developed by Pepper & Gaudi (2005) to account for two effects of particular importance to transit surveys targeting star clusters: correlated ("red") noise in photometric time series and magnitude limits imposed by the need for radial velocity follow-up and confirmation. The original formalism, which estimates the expected number of detectable transiting planets as a function of survey parameters, assumes purely uncorrelated (white) photometric noise and does not explicitly account for the additional constraints that arise when candidate host stars must be bright enough for precise radial velocity measurements to confirm planetary nature and measure masses. We generalize the detection signal-to-noise calculation to incorporate a red-noise component parameterized in a manner consistent with observational studies of ground- and space-based photometry, and we introduce a radial velocity magnitude cutoff that excludes stars too faint for spectroscopic follow-up with a given telescope aperture and instrument. We derive updated expressions for the expected planet yield as a function of survey depth, cadence, stellar density, cluster distance, and telescope characteristics, and we explore how these two effects individually and jointly reshape the predicted yields relative to the white-noise-only case. We find that red noise systematically suppresses sensitivity to small planets and long periods, effectively raising the detection threshold in a manner that depends on the ratio of the correlated noise timescale to the transit duration, while the radial velocity magnitude limit imposes a hard cut in stellar brightness that can dominate the yield for distant or crowded clusters where only the brightest stars are amenable to mass measurement. We apply this updated formalism to representative cluster survey scenarios, illustrating how the interplay between photometric precision, red noise, cluster distance, and telescope aperture determines the optimal survey design for maximizing the number of confirmable transiting planets. This framework provides a practical tool for planning and interpreting transit surveys of star clusters, where both systematic noise and follow-up feasibility are often limiting factors not captured by idealized white-noise yield calculations.

counterfactuals.output:
# Abstract

Transit surveys of homogeneous stellar populations, such as open clusters, offer unique advantages for constraining planet occurrence rates by minimizing systematic variations in stellar properties across the target sample. However, the detection of planetary transits—particularly small-radius planets such as hot Neptunes—is critically sensitive to the noise properties of the underlying photometric time series on transit-relevant time-scales (typically 1–10 hours). While white noise contributions are readily characterized and mitigated through standard photometric techniques, correlated ("red") noise arising from stellar variability, instrumental systematics, and atmospheric effects can substantially degrade detection sensitivity in ways not captured by simple Gaussian noise estimates.

In this work, we investigate the impact of red noise on transit detection probability within simulated and archival photometric datasets of open cluster members, focusing on the implications for identifying hot Neptune-sized planets (radii of 2–6 Earth radii). We construct synthetic light curves incorporating realistic red noise components calibrated to observed stellar variability in cluster populations, and we inject transit signals consistent with expected hot Neptune parameters. Using a matched-filter detection algorithm, we quantify the reduction in detection efficiency as a function of red noise amplitude and correlation time-scale relative to the idealized white-noise-only case.

We find that even modest levels of red noise—consistent with those observed in ground- and space-based cluster surveys—can suppress detection probabilities for hot Neptune transits by factors of several, with the effect most pronounced when the red noise correlation time-scale approaches the transit duration. This degradation disproportionately affects smaller planets, introducing a size-dependent bias into inferred occurrence rates that is difficult to disentangle from intrinsic astrophysical trends without careful noise characterization. We further show that standard signal-to-noise metrics assuming white noise statistics systematically overestimate detection completeness by up to an order of magnitude in red-noise-dominated regimes.

These results have direct implications for planet occurrence rate studies in open clusters, where sample sizes are often small and biases in detection completeness can significantly skew inferred demographics. We recommend that future cluster transit surveys incorporate empirically-derived red noise models specific to the target population when computing detection probabilities, and we provide a framework for correcting completeness estimates accordingly. This is particularly critical for hot Neptune studies, where the combination of small planetary radii and the need to resolve the "Neptune desert" demands accurate assessment of survey sensitivity as a function of both planet size and orbital period.

# Abstract

Transit surveys targeting stellar clusters offer unique advantages for exoplanet demographic studies, including well-constrained stellar ages, metallicities, and distances. However, yield predictions for such surveys have historically relied on idealized noise models that assume purely white (uncorrelated) photometric noise, leading to systematic overestimates of detection completeness. In this work, we present a revised framework for predicting transit survey yields in dense stellar fields that explicitly incorporates correlated noise sources—including residual systematics from differential image motion, blending in crowded fields, and intra-pixel sensitivity variations—alongside realistic constraints imposed by radial velocity (RV) follow-up requirements for planet confirmation and mass measurement.

We model correlated noise using a wavelet-based decomposition that captures both time-correlated ("red") noise and its impact on transit signal-to-noise calculations across a range of stellar magnitudes and cluster crowding conditions. We further couple these detection completeness estimates to a follow-up feasibility module that accounts for host star brightness, rotational broadening, and achievable RV precision, since cluster members are often faint, rapidly rotating, and reside in fields with high stellar density that complicates spectroscopic extraction. We apply this framework to simulated surveys of open clusters spanning a range of ages (10 Myr–4 Gyr) and distances (100–2000 pc), representative of upcoming and ongoing photometric monitoring campaigns.

Our results demonstrate that correlated noise reduces effective detection completeness by 15–40% relative to white-noise-only predictions, with the largest effects for small planets (R_p < 2 R_⊕) around faint (V > 16) stars. When combined with RV follow-up constraints, we find that the fraction of detected planets amenable to mass measurement using next-generation spectrographs drops below 20% for clusters beyond 500 pc, fundamentally limiting the statistical power of distant cluster surveys for measuring planet mass-radius relations as a function of age. We provide updated yield predictions and a public toolkit for survey design that incorporates these effects, and we discuss implications for optimizing target selection and exposure time allocation in current and future cluster-focused transit surveys, including K2, TESS, and PLATO cluster campaigns.

# Summary: Noise Budget and Detection Statistics for Box-Shaped Transits in Wide-Field Surveys

## Overview
This study revisits the theoretical framework for detecting planetary transits using simplified "box-shaped" light curve models, with particular attention to how detection sensitivity scales with stellar mass. The work is motivated by the practical constraints of small-aperture, wide-field photometric surveys targeting nearby open clusters and field stars.

## Key Components of the Re-derivation

**Noise Budget**
The study reconstructs the various noise sources relevant to ground-based, small-aperture transit surveys:
- **Photon (shot) noise** from the target star, scaling with stellar flux
- **Sky background noise**, particularly significant for wide-field instruments with larger effective pixel scales
- **Scintillation noise**, which depends on telescope aperture, exposure time, and airmass
- **Read noise and dark current**, relevant for the detector systematics
- **Systematic/red noise floors**, often dominant for bright stars observed at high cadence

These terms are combined into a single effective noise model as a function of stellar apparent magnitude, spectral type, and instrumental parameters (aperture size, pixel scale, exposure time).

## Transit Signal Modeling

**Box-Shaped Approximation**
Rather than using full limb-darkened transit light curves, the analysis adopts an idealized box (trapezoidal/rectangular) transit shape, characterized by:
- Transit depth δ ∝ (R_p/R_star)²
- Transit duration T_dur, dependent on orbital period, stellar density, and impact parameter
- Ingress/egress timescales (often simplified or neglected in the box approximation)

This simplification allows for analytic tractability while retaining the essential dependence on stellar and planetary parameters.

## Mass-Dependent Scaling

A central result of the paper is the explicit calculation of how detection statistics (e.g., **signal-to-noise ratio, or SNR**, and related quantities like the Box Least-Squares detection statistic) scale with stellar mass M_star:

- **Transit depth** scales as δ ∝ (R_p/R_star)², and since R_star correlates with M_star along the main sequence, δ effectively becomes a decreasing function of M_star for fixed planet radius
- **Transit duration** T_dur ∝ (P)^{1/3} × (ρ_star)^{-1/3}, introducing further stellar-density dependence
- **Number of transits observed** during a survey depends on orbital period and survey baseline, folding into the cumulative SNR
- **Noise per data point** depends on stellar brightness, which for a flux-limited or magnitude-limited survey sample correlates with M_star (via mass-luminosity relation)

Combining these, the paper derives a **combined scaling relation** for the total detection SNR (or equivalently, the BLS statistic) as a function of stellar mass, showing that survey sensitivity is not uniform across spectral types — typically favoring detection around lower-mass stars (larger relative transit depths) but working against them if photon noise dominates due to intrinsic faintness.

## Application to Cluster Surveys

The derivation is specifically framed for **nearby open clusters** observed with **small-aperture, wide-field telescopes** (typical of many ground-based transit surveys), where:
- Crowding and blending are relevant systematics
- The stellar mass function of the cluster determines the target sample
- Survey duration is fixed by cluster observability (seasonal visibility, baseline)
- Detection efficiency must be computed as a function of stellar mass to properly assess the **completeness function** for planet occurrence rate studies

## Purpose and Utility

The re-derivation serves as a **foundational reference** for:
1. Computing detection efficiency maps (mass vs. period vs. planet radius) for specific cluster survey datasets
2. Interpreting non-detections or upper limits on planet occurrence rates in clusters
3. Providing a transparent, analytic (rather than purely numerical/injection-recovery) framework for understanding survey biases
4. Facilitating comparison between different surveys with varying instrumental setups (aperture, cadence, precision) by normalizing detection statistics to a common mass-dependent framework

---

*Note: Without access to the specific paper referenced, this summary represents the standard structure and content expected of such a methodological study based on established practices in the transit survey literature (e.g., analyses following Pepper & Gaudi, Fressin et al., or similar works on ground-based cluster transit surveys such as PISCES, Monitor, or similar programs).*

counterfactuals.output:
# Abstract

Star clusters offer unique environments for exoplanet transit surveys, providing coeval, chemically homogeneous stellar populations with well-constrained ages and distances. However, the photometric precision required to detect planetary transits in dense stellar fields is often compromised by correlated noise sources, including blending, crowding, and systematic instrumental effects that do not average down with additional observations. We investigate the impact of constant correlated noise on transit detection efficiency across stellar clusters spanning a range of distances, ages, and stellar masses, with particular attention to how noise correlations affect detectability as a function of host star mass.

Our simulations demonstrate that correlated noise floors disproportionately suppress transit detection around higher-mass stars, where the transit depth-to-noise ratio is intrinsically reduced due to larger stellar radii. This effect systematically biases cluster transit surveys toward preferential sensitivity for lower-mass stars, even when accounting for the increased frequency of large planets around evolved, higher-mass hosts. We quantify this detection bias across a grid of cluster distances and noise properties, showing that surveys targeting distant clusters (>100 pc) suffer substantial losses in sensitivity to giant planets around solar-type and higher-mass stars once realistic correlated noise levels are included, even under optimistic assumptions for time baseline and photometric cadence.

In contrast, we find that nearby open clusters (d < 100 pc) retain strong prospects for detecting close-in Neptune-mass planets ("hot Neptunes") via transit photometry, owing to the favorable scaling of signal-to-noise with proximity that partially offsets correlated noise limitations. We further show that combining transit surveys with dedicated radial velocity (RV) follow-up campaigns significantly enhances detection completeness and enables robust planetary mass measurements for these systems. This synergy is particularly powerful for nearby clusters, where target brightness permits efficient RV monitoring. We conclude that next-generation surveys of nearby clusters, combining high-precision photometry with strategic RV follow-up, represent the most promising pathway for characterizing hot Neptune populations in coeval environments, while cautioning that correlated noise must be carefully modeled when interpreting non-detections of giant planets around higher-mass cluster members in more distant surveys.
